meta.description: Quantitative finance interview prep platform. Problems are scraped from quantprof.org, processed, and embedded directly into the HTML. A Python script (update_deploy.py) re-embeds fresh JSON and pushes to GitHub Pages automatically.
meta.dataFlow: scraper → quantprof_problems.json → update_deploy.py → index.html (embedded) → GitHub Pages

sync.fallback: localStorage for all three when offline

problems.title: Non-empty Intersection
problems.question: Five intervals are chosen uniformly at random from [0,1]. What is the probability that they all share a common point?
problems.hint1: Think about what it means for all intervals to share a common point.
problems.hint2: Consider the maximum of the left endpoints and the minimum of the right endpoints.
problems.solution: The intervals share a common point iff max(l_i) ≤ min(r_i). By symmetry this reduces to a clean combinatorial argument.

problems.title: Gambler's Ruin
problems.question: A gambler starts with $k and plays a fair coin-flip game, winning or losing $1 each round. What is the probability they reach $N before going broke?
problems.hint1: Set up a system of equations using first-step analysis.
problems.hint2: For a fair game, the solution is linear.
problems.solution: By the optional stopping theorem, the expected wealth is a martingale, so P(reach N) = k/N.

problems.title: Expected Maximum of Uniform
problems.question: You draw n samples independently from Uniform[0,1]. What is the expected value of the maximum?
problems.hint1: Use the CDF of the maximum of n uniforms.
problems.solution: E[X_(n)] = n/(n+1) via integration of the order statistic CDF.

problems.title: Ant on a Rubber Band
problems.question: An ant walks 1 cm/s on a rubber band that stretches 1 m/s uniformly. The band starts at 1 m. Does the ant ever reach the end?
problems.hint1: Think about the fraction of the band the ant has covered, not the absolute position.
problems.solution: Track the ant's fractional position. Each second it gains 1/(L_t) fraction. The total gain is the harmonic series, which diverges — so the ant eventually reaches 1.

problems.title: Covariance of Order Statistics
problems.question: For n iid Uniform[0,1] random variables, find Cov(X_(i), X_(j)) for i ≤ j.
problems.hint1: Use the joint density of order statistics.
problems.solution: Cov(X_(i), X_(j)) = i(n-j+1) / ((n+1)^2(n+2)) from standard order statistic theory.

problems.title: Random Walk Returns to Origin
problems.question: In a 1D simple random walk, what is the probability of ever returning to the origin?
problems.hint1: Use the recurrence criterion for random walks.
problems.solution: The 1D simple random walk is recurrent: it returns to the origin with probability 1. This follows from the divergence of sum 1/sqrt(n).

problems.title: Fair Coin from Biased Coin
problems.question: You have a biased coin with unknown bias p. How do you simulate a fair coin flip?
problems.hint1: Flip the coin twice. Some outcomes are symmetric.
problems.solution: Flip twice. If HT → output H, TH → output T, HH or TT → repeat. Both HT and TH have probability p(1-p), so the output is unbiased.

problems.title: Black-Scholes Put-Call Parity
problems.question: Derive the put-call parity relationship for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock.
problems.hint1: Consider two portfolios that have the same payoff at expiry.
problems.hint2: One portfolio: long call + cash Ke^{-rT}. Other: long put + long stock.
problems.solution: At expiry both portfolios pay max(S_T, K). By no-arbitrage they must have the same value today: C + Ke^{-rT} = P + S, i.e. C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}.
